problem: The answer says code-mixing brings a second language and a second script into the sentence. Its own Hinglish example, "kal meeting cancel hai", is written in Roman script, not Devanagari, so there is no second script. Script mixing (writing Hindi in Devanagari inside an English sentence, or romanised Hindi) is a separate problem from code-mixing, and a student would carry the wrong claim into the exam.
fix: A spelling mistake leaves the word recognisable to a close match. Code-mixing swaps in words from a second language inside the same sentence, so the vocabulary, the morphology and often the word order all shift at once, and a model trained on one language has no matching evidence. Hinglish is usually typed in Roman script, so the script may stay the same while the language changes; script mixing, where Devanagari and Latin characters appear together, is an extra problem on top of that.

problem: "The chicken is ready to eat" is presented as the case where "the structure is fixed". In the two readings the chicken fills different roles: it is the eater in one and the thing eaten in the other, so the argument structure differs, and many texts call this an argument-structure or control ambiguity rather than a purely semantic one. Telling students the structure is fixed here can mislead them.
fix: For fixed structure with two meanings, use a scope example: "Every student read a book" (one particular book for all, or a possibly different book each). Keep "The chicken is ready to eat" only if it is described as an ambiguity in who does the eating, that is, in the argument structure of "eat", not as a case of fixed structure. Change the Quiz Q4(ii) answer to match.

problem: The lead defines NLP as turning human text into something a computer can act on, but Section 1 says the input is text or speech and the output can be a translation or a reply, and Section 2 includes speech transcription and text-to-speech. A student reading only the lead will think NLP is text-only and spoken input belongs elsewhere.
fix: Say the input is text or speech and the output is a structure another program can use: a label, a tree, a translation, a spoken reply. Keep the bank and Hindi examples as they are.
